The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For a measure $\mu$, write
$$L^1(\mu):=\{f:X\to\mathbb C:\ f \text{ is integrable}\}.$$
Here **integrable** is the notion introduced in
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

On this page $L^1(\mu)$ is the class of integrable representatives. The later
Banach-space page will pass to almost-everywhere equivalence classes.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$
If $F\in AC[a,b]$ and $h$ is Lipschitz on $F([a,b])$, then $h\circ F\in AC[a,b]$.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

derivations.claim: If $a=b$, both hypotheses reduce to $u(a)\le A$, which is the claimed bound. Hence assume $a<b$ and first consider the forward inequality. Define $C(t)=\int_a^t\ell(s)\,ds$ and $V(t)=A+\int_a^t\ell(s)u(s)\,ds$. Continuity of $u$ on the compact interval makes it bounded, so $\ell u\in L^1$. By [F2], both $C$ and $V$ are absolutely continuous, and the hypothesis says $0\le u(t)\le V(t)$. The range of $C$ is contained in the compact interval $[0,C(b)]$; [F6] makes $r\mapsto e^{-r}$ Lipschitz there. Thus $e^{-C}$ is absolutely continuous by [F4], and $W(t):=e^{-C(t)}V(t)$ is absolutely continuous by [F5].

Since $\ell,\ell u\in L^1[a,b]$, [F9] gives $C'=\ell$ and $V'=\ell u$ almost everywhere. By [F3], the absolutely continuous function $W$ has an integrable derivative and is the integral of that derivative after its initial value. Intersecting these full-measure sets, at every remaining point [F7] gives $$W'=e^{-C}(V'-C'V)=e^{-C}\ell(u-V)\le0,$$ since $u\le V$ and $\ell\ge0$. Therefore [F3] yields $W(t)-W(a)=\int_a^tW'(s)\,ds\le0$. As $W(a)=A$ and $u(t)\le V(t)$, we obtain $u(t)\le V(t)\le A e^{C(t)}$, the claimed forward estimate.

By step 1.1, assume $a<b$. Set $\widetilde u(r)=u(a+b-r)$ and $\widetilde\ell(r)=\ell(a+b-r)$. By [F8], reflection preserves measurability and integrability and gives $\int_a^r\widetilde\ell(q)\widetilde u(q)\,dq=\int_{a+b-r}^b\ell(s)u(s)\,ds$. Thus $\widetilde u(r)\le A+\int_a^r\widetilde\ell(q)\widetilde u(q)\,dq$. The forward result in steps 1.1–2.1 applies to these continuous and integrable functions. Substituting $r=a+b-t$ into its bound gives $u(t)\le A\exp(\int_t^b\ell(s)\,ds)$.

Let $a\le b$, let $A\ge0$, let $u:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, and let $\ell:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)$ be Lebesgue measurable with $\int_a^b\ell(s)\,ds<\infty$. If
$$u(t)\le A+\int_a^t\ell(s)u(s)\,ds\qquad(a\le t\le b),$$
then
$$u(t)\le A\exp\!\left(\int_a^t\ell(s)\,ds\right)\qquad(a\le t\le b).$$
If instead $u(t)\le A+\int_t^b\ell(s)u(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[a,b]$, then
$$u(t)\le A\exp\!\left(\int_t^b\ell(s)\,ds\right)\qquad(a\le t\le b).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $J$ be a nonempty compact interval and $n\ge1$. Continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on $J$ are complete in the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(x,y):=\sup_{t\in J}\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $F:D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and
$C^1$ in the state variable. Fix data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ and a compact time
interval $I=[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ on which the corresponding solutions through nearby
initial states all exist. Then the solution map

$$\Phi:I\times U_0\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad \Phi(t,y)=x(t;y),$$

is $C^1$ in the initial-state variable $y$ on some neighbourhood $U_0$ of
$x_0$. For each $y\in U_0$, the derivative matrix
$D_y\Phi(t,y)$ is the solution of the variational equation along $t\mapsto x(t;y)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

For a measure $\mu$, write
$$L^1(\mu):=\{f:X\to\mathbb C:\ f \text{ is integrable}\}.$$
Here **integrable** is the notion introduced in
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

On this page $L^1(\mu)$ is the class of integrable representatives. The later
Banach-space page will pass to almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $x \in X$.
Neighbourhoods are as in [[def-neighbourhood-top]].

$f$ is **continuous at $x$** if for every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ in $Y$ the
preimage $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ in $X$.

$f$ is **continuous** if it is continuous at every point of $X$.

**The same condition with open sets only.** $f$ is continuous at $x$ if and only
if for every open $V \subseteq Y$ with $f(x) \in V$ there is an open
$U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ and $f[U] \subseteq V$. Indeed, if $f$ is
continuous at $x$ and $V$ is such an open set, then $V$ is a neighbourhood of
$f(x)$, so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ and contains an open $U \ni x$,
which satisfies $f[U] \subseteq V$. Conversely, given the displayed condition and
a neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$, fix open $V_0$ with $f(x) \in V_0 \subseteq V$ and
then open $U \ni x$ with $f[U] \subseteq V_0$; then $x \in U \subseteq f^{-1}[V_0] \subseteq f^{-1}[V]$,
so $f^{-1}[V]$ is a neighbourhood of $x$. Both forms are used below and are the
same statement written twice.

**Preimage, not image.** $f^{-1}[V] = \{\, x \in X : f(x) \in V \,\}$
is the preimage in the sense of [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]] and is
defined for every function, invertible or not; no inverse function is being
asserted to exist. Continuity is a condition on preimages throughout, and the
corresponding conditions on images define the *open* and *closed* maps of a later
item, which are different notions.

derivations.claim: Fix a compact parameter set $K$. Let $C(t)=\int_0^tL_K(s)ds$. By [F4] and [F12], $C$ is continuous and nondecreasing on $[0,T]$, and [F6] makes it uniformly continuous. Choose a finite partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$ with mesh small enough that $C(t_{i+1})-C(t_i)=\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}L_K(s)ds\le1/2$ on each cell. On a cell $J=[t_i,t_{i+1}]$, with initial value $z_i$, consider the closed supremum-norm ball of radius $R=2(1+|z_i|+\int_Ja_K)$ about the constant curve $z_i$. For $z$ in that ball define $\mathcal Tz(t)=z_i+\int_{t_i}^t b(s,z(s),y)\,ds.$ The integrand is continuous by [F13], so $\mathcal Tz$ is continuous.

Put $q_J=\int_JL_K\le1/2$. The triangle inequality and spatial Lipschitz bound with $x'=0$ give $|b(s,z(s),y)|\le a_K(s)+L_K(s)|z(s)|$ almost everywhere. Hence $\|\mathcal Tz-z_i\|_\infty\le\int_Ja_K+q_J(|z_i|+R)\le R,$ so the ball maps into itself. For two curves, [F3] and the Lipschitz bound give $\|\mathcal Tz-\mathcal Tw\|_\infty\le q_J\|z-w\|_\infty$. The ball is nonempty and complete by [F1], so [F2] gives a unique fixed point, which solves the integral equation and hence the ODE on $J$ by [F5]. Applying this construction on the finite partition and using uniqueness at each shared endpoint gives a unique solution on all of $[0,T]$.

For solutions $x(t),x'(t)$ with the same $y$ and initial values $x_0,x'_0$, subtract their integral equations and use [F3] to obtain $|x(t)-x'(t)|\le|x_0-x'_0|+\int_0^t L_K(s)|x(s)-x'(s)|\,ds.$ The forward clause of the integrable-coefficient Grönwall lemma gives the factor $\exp(\int_0^tL_K)$, proving uniqueness and the forward Lipschitz bound. Applying the same existence and uniqueness construction to the reversed drift $\bar b(s,z,y)=-b(T-s,z,y)$ gives a backward solution from any terminal value; uniqueness shows that its time-zero map is the inverse of $T_y$ and the same estimate gives the inverse Lipschitz bound.

From the integral equation and [F3], $|x_y(t;x_0)|\le |x_0|+\int_0^T a_K+\int_0^tL_K(s)|x_y(s;x_0)|ds$. The integrable Grönwall estimate therefore gives $|x_y(t;x_0)|\le(|x_0|+\int_0^Ta_K)\exp(\int_0^TL_K)$, uniformly in $t$ and for $x_0,y$ in compact sets. Thus all such trajectories lie in a common compact state ball. The drift is uniformly continuous on the product of this ball, $[0,T]$, and $K$ by [F6]. Choose a compact $K$ containing a convergent sequence $y_n$ and its limit. For $(x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)$, subtract the integral equations along $x_{y_n}(\cdot;x_n)$ and $x_y(\cdot;x)$; the result is bounded by $|x_n-x|+T\omega(|y_n-y|)+\int_0^tL_K(s)|x_{y_n}(s;x_n)-x_y(s;x)|ds$, where $\omega(r)\to0$ is a modulus from [F6]. Grönwall proves uniform convergence of the paths. Repeating for the reversed drift proves continuity of the inverse map in initial value and parameter.

In the C$^1$ clause, fix $y$ and an initial state $x_0$. Steps 2.1 and 4.1 give common existence and continuous dependence for nearby initial states on $[0,T]$. Their trajectories and the line segments joining corresponding states lie in a common compact state ball, so $[0,T]$ times that ball is a compact state tube in the field domain. On this tube $D_xb$ is bounded and uniformly continuous. The difference-quotient argument in [F7] therefore applies on $[0,T]$: the map $x_0\mapsto x_y(t;x_0)$ is $C^1$ for every $t$, and its derivative is the solution of the variational equation. Apply the same argument to the reversed drift $\bar b(s,x,y)=-b(T-s,x,y)$; its time-$T$ map is $T_y^{-1}$ by uniqueness in step 3.1. The two maps are consequently $C^1$ inverses, so $T_y$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.

Write $B(t)=D_xb(t,x_y(t;x_0),y)$ and $A(t)=A_y(t,x_0)$. Step 4.2 applied on each restricted interval $[0,t]$ shows that the time-$t$ flow is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, so $A(t)$ is invertible for every $t$ (and $A(0)=I_d$). The path $B$ is continuous. By [F5], $G(t):=\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}B(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(0,T)$ with $G'(t)=\operatorname{tr}B(t)$ and has the corresponding one-sided endpoint derivatives. For $0<t<T$, the total-derivative chain rule [F8] and the invertible-matrix formula in [F9], applied to the variational equation $A'=BA$, give $$\frac{d}{dt}\det A(t)=D\det(A(t))[A'(t)]=\det A(t)\operatorname{tr}(A(t)^{-1}B(t)A(t))=\det A(t)\operatorname{tr}B(t),$$ using cyclicity of trace; continuity extends this identity to the endpoints. By the scalar product and chain rules in [F11], $e^{-G(t)}\det A(t)$ has derivative zero on $(0,T)$, so the mean-value theorem makes it constant on $[0,T]$. Its value at $t=0$ is $1$; hence $\det A(t)=\exp(G(t))$, the asserted Liouville formula.

If $\eta(dx)=q(x)dx$, then for every Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $T_y{}_{\#}\eta(E)=\int_{T_y^{-1}(E)}q(x)dx.$ Apply [F10] to the diffeomorphism $T_y^{-1}$ and the nonnegative measurable integrand $x\mapsto\mathbf1_{T_y^{-1}(E)}(x)q(x)$. This rewrites the last integral as $\int_Eq(T_y^{-1}(z))|\det DT_y^{-1}(z)|dz$, which proves the stated density formula. The first part of the Statement used no C$^1$ assumption; therefore global Lipschitzness alone yields only the bi-Lipschitz flow conclusion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions
$x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then
$(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d,m\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly continuous on the product Euclidean domain. Suppose that for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ there are nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $a_K,L_K\in L^1([0,T])$ such that for almost every $t$, simultaneously for all $y\in K$ and $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,0,y)|\le a_K(t),\qquad |b(t,x,y)-b(t,x',y)|\le L_K(t)|x-x'|.$$
Here $L^1([0,T])$ means the functions have finite Lebesgue integral of their absolute values. Then for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y\in\mathbb R^m$ there is a unique continuously differentiable solution $x_y(\cdot;x_0)$ of
$$\dot x(t)=b(t,x(t),y),\qquad x(0)=x_0,$$
on all of $[0,T]$. Its terminal map $T_y(x_0):=x_y(T;x_0)$ is a bijection with jointly continuous forward and inverse maps in $(x_0,y)$, and for all $x_0,x_1$ and $y\in K$,
$$|T_y(x_0)-T_y(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|,\qquad |T_y^{-1}(x_0)-T_y^{-1}(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|.$$

In the separate C$^1$ clause, suppose additionally that the state derivative $D_xb$ exists and is jointly continuous. Then for fixed $y$, $T_y$ is a bijection and both $T_y$ and its inverse are continuously differentiable. For a measurable map $S$ and a measure $\mu$, define its image measure by $S_{\#}\mu(E):=\mu(S^{-1}(E))$. The derivative $A_y(t,x_0):=D_{x_0}x_y(t;x_0)$ solves
$$\dot A_y(t,x_0)=D_xb(t,x_y(t;x_0),y)A_y(t,x_0),\qquad A_y(0,x_0)=I_d,$$
with Liouville formula
$$\det A_y(t,x_0)=\exp\!\left(\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}D_xb(s,x_y(s;x_0),y)\,ds\right).$$
Consequently, if a probability measure $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ has Lebesgue density $q$, meaning $\eta(E)=\int_Eq(x)\,dx$ for Borel $E$, the image measure $T_y{}_{\#}\eta$ has density
$$z\longmapsto q(T_y^{-1}(z))\,|\det D T_y^{-1}(z)|.$$
The global Lipschitz clause alone gives a bi-Lipschitz flow and does not assert a Jacobian density formula.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

derivations.claim: By [A1], [F1], and [F2], the supplied $\pi_y$ is a disintegration of $\pi$ given its second coordinate. For Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, define $\kappa_y(A):=\eta(\{x:T_y(x)\in A\})=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbf1_A(T_y(x))\,\eta(dx)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with its norm topology, $D\subseteq X$ a Borel forward-map domain, and $\mu_0$ a Borel probability measure on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Write $\mu_{0,D}$ for its restriction to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D):=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. A likelihood potential is a function $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is the trace of $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ on $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Viewing $\Phi$ via the inclusion $(-\infty,+\infty]\hookrightarrow\overline{\mathbb R}$, it is also product-measurable as an extended-real-valued map because for every Borel set $B\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$, $\Phi^{-1}(B)=\Phi^{-1}(B\cap(-\infty,+\infty])$ is measurable by the definition of the trace sigma-algebra. Here $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded; set $e^{-\infty}=0$. The scalar map $t\mapsto e^{-t}$ on this range is continuous at finite $t$, and is continuous at $+\infty$: given $\varepsilon>0$, the limit supplies $a\in\mathbb R$ such that $t>a$ implies $e^{-t}<\varepsilon$, and the order-topology neighborhood $(a,+\infty]$ maps into $[0,\varepsilon)$. Hence it is Borel, so $L_\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$, $L_\Phi(u;y):=e^{-\Phi(u;y)}$, is product-measurable by composition, and each section $u\mapsto L_\Phi(u;y)$ is nonnegative and measurable. Define its evidence by
$$
Z_\Phi(y):=\int_D L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)\in[0,+\infty].
$$
For each fixed $y$ with $0<Z_\Phi(y)<+\infty$, define the normalized fiberwise update on $A\in\mathcal B(D)$ by
$$\Pi^y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_\Phi(u;y)\,\mu_{0,D}(du)}{Z_\Phi(y)}.$$
No normalized fiberwise update is defined by this formula when $Z_\Phi(y)=0$ or $Z_\Phi(y)=+\infty$.

For a data-indexed claim, an observation model and its version convention must also be specified. In the dominated case, let $Q$ be a proper probability kernel from $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, and suppose $Q(u,B)=\int_B L_\Phi(u;y)\,\nu(dy)$ for every $u\in D$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$. Then $Z_\Phi$ is the density of the prior-predictive data law with respect to $\nu$; a data-indexed conditional-law version uses $\Pi^y$ when $0<Z_\Phi(y)<\infty$ and the prior $\mu_{0,D}$ when $Z_\Phi(y)$ is zero or infinite. These filled fibers have zero prior-predictive mass, and their chosen values are not normalized fiberwise updates. More generally, for a proper Bayesian model with standard-Borel parameter space $(D,\mathcal B(D))$ and data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ (each measurably isomorphic to the Borel space of a Polish space), the Axiom of Choice guarantees a data-indexed posterior kernel; its values are unique as probability measures outside one data-marginal-null set, and values on that null set remain version choices. The dominated construction is choice-free; the separate standard-Borel existence branch assumes the Axiom of Choice.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d,m\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$ be jointly continuous on the product Euclidean domain. Suppose that for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ there are nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable $a_K,L_K\in L^1([0,T])$ such that for almost every $t$, simultaneously for all $y\in K$ and $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,0,y)|\le a_K(t),\qquad |b(t,x,y)-b(t,x',y)|\le L_K(t)|x-x'|.$$
Here $L^1([0,T])$ means the functions have finite Lebesgue integral of their absolute values. Then for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y\in\mathbb R^m$ there is a unique continuously differentiable solution $x_y(\cdot;x_0)$ of
$$\dot x(t)=b(t,x(t),y),\qquad x(0)=x_0,$$
on all of $[0,T]$. Its terminal map $T_y(x_0):=x_y(T;x_0)$ is a bijection with jointly continuous forward and inverse maps in $(x_0,y)$, and for all $x_0,x_1$ and $y\in K$,
$$|T_y(x_0)-T_y(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|,\qquad |T_y^{-1}(x_0)-T_y^{-1}(x_1)|\le e^{\int_0^T L_K(t)dt}|x_0-x_1|.$$

In the separate C$^1$ clause, suppose additionally that the state derivative $D_xb$ exists and is jointly continuous. Then for fixed $y$, $T_y$ is a bijection and both $T_y$ and its inverse are continuously differentiable. For a measurable map $S$ and a measure $\mu$, define its image measure by $S_{\#}\mu(E):=\mu(S^{-1}(E))$. The derivative $A_y(t,x_0):=D_{x_0}x_y(t;x_0)$ solves
$$\dot A_y(t,x_0)=D_xb(t,x_y(t;x_0),y)A_y(t,x_0),\qquad A_y(0,x_0)=I_d,$$
with Liouville formula
$$\det A_y(t,x_0)=\exp\!\left(\int_0^t\operatorname{tr}D_xb(s,x_y(s;x_0),y)\,ds\right).$$
Consequently, if a probability measure $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ has Lebesgue density $q$, meaning $\eta(E)=\int_Eq(x)\,dx$ for Borel $E$, the image measure $T_y{}_{\#}\eta$ has density
$$z\longmapsto q(T_y^{-1}(z))\,|\det D T_y^{-1}(z)|.$$
The global Lipschitz clause alone gives a bi-Lipschitz flow and does not assert a Jacobian density formula.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$, where $d,m\ge1$, and let $\pi_Y(B):=\pi(\mathbb R^d\times B)$ be its second marginal. Let $\eta$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$, and let $y\mapsto\pi_y$ be a probability kernel satisfying
$$\pi(A\times B)=\int_B\pi_y(A)\,\pi_Y(dy)$$
for all Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$. Suppose $T:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^m$ is Borel and triangular, $T(x,y)=(T_y(x),y)$, with each $T_y$ a Borel bijection, and define the image measure by $T_{\#}\mu(E):=\mu(T^{-1}(E))$. If
$$T_{\#}(\eta\otimes\pi_Y)=\pi,$$
then $T_y{}_{\#}\eta=\pi_y$ as probability measures for $\pi_Y$-almost every $y$. By disintegration on standard Borel spaces, such a kernel $\pi_y$ exists and is unique outside one $\pi_Y$-null set. In a proper Bayesian model, when $\pi$ is the joint parameter/data law, this conditional kernel is the posterior kernel; the conclusion says an exact triangular transport maps the reference law to the data-conditioned posterior for almost every datum.

For the triangular terminal flow in the preceding ODE lemma, joint continuity supplies the Borel map and each fiber is a bijection. The theorem requires only the exact joint pushforward identity; it does not require a density or a Jacobian formula.

derivations.claim: Every training quantity in [F1] is formed from $X_0$, $(X_1,Y)$, independent time, the interpolant and its endpoint difference. These are all available under the specified sampling interface, so no likelihood value is needed to form a CFM training example.

The density-based MH acceptance ratio in [F2] contains the unnormalized posterior target. By [F3] its likelihood contribution is the ratio of likelihoods, which sampling access alone does not supply in general; [F4]'s proposal density does not supply it either. This is an interface limitation rather than an impossibility in every specified model: if the likelihood is independent of the parameter, its ratio is one wherever the forward flow is positive, and the prior and proposal ratios suffice. Thus additional knowledge of an evaluable ratio can permit this correction even without separate likelihood evaluations.

[F5] is a separate route: if the exact joint transport identity is established, the disintegration theorem gives the posterior fiber law on its full-measure set; a fixed query datum must lie in that set unless equality is separately established there. The present example makes no claim that finite training establishes the identity, and supplying a likelihood estimator would change the MH interface.
